query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting Mo with Nb in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy will lower the overall electronegativity difference—thereby improving dislocation mobility and plasticity—while the Nb substitution preserves strong solid solution strengthening, thus maintaining high room‐temperature compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic disordered BCC NbZrTiHfMo alloy with high Mo content causing high electronegativity difference and limited plasticity.
generation.intervention: Reduce the Mo content by a controlled amount (e.g., 25–50%) and replace it on a one-to-one atomic basis with Nb.
generation.conditions: The alloy must remain a disordered BCC phase at room temperature and the Mo substitution level must be moderate (not exceeding ~50% replacement) so that the solid solution strengthening effect is preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: A lowered electronegativity difference and reduced local bond polarity leading to a more homogeneous lattice without significantly altering the BCC structure.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a lower electronegativity compared to Mo; by partially replacing Mo with Nb, the overall chemical heterogeneity that impedes dislocation motion is reduced. This adjustment permits increased dislocation activity (enhanced plasticity) while the remaining Mo and the added Nb continue to contribute to the solid solution strengthening that gives the alloy its high yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: A revised alloy composition exhibiting a room-temperature compressive yield strength comparable to the original (~1719 MPa) but with an improved plasticity (i.e., increased plastic strain before failure) relative to the equiatomic alloy.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy with a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa and notably reduced room-temperature plasticity.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the Mo reduction does not exceed ~50% of its original content; excessive replacement may undermine the necessary solid solution strengthening and could induce phase instability.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain at what precise substitution level the balance between plasticity and strength is optimal, and the response may be sensitive to small compositional changes. Additionally, the interplay of other elements with Nb and Mo could have unforeseen effects on dislocation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of alloys where Mo is partially substituted by Nb in increments (e.g., replace 10%, 25%, and 50% of the Mo content by atomic percent), while keeping the overall atomic ratio for the other elements constant. Confirm that all samples maintain a disordered BCC phase via XRD.
measurements: Plastic strain at fracture under compression
Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, TEM) for dislocation structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with partial Mo replacement by Nb do not exhibit at least a 20% improvement in plasticity (measured as plastic strain before fracture) while maintaining compressive yield strength within 10% of the baseline (1719 MPa), then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

However, the melting point of Nickel-base superalloy limits the application itself above 1200 °C. Therefore, it is necessary to develop new refractory alloys, especially for applications at temperatures higher than 1200 °C.
In 2004, Professor Yeh and his group published the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention.
